# What a cluster is (and why your laptop isn't one) {#sec-cluster}

::: {.tldr}
A cluster is a few hundred computers that share storage and a waitlist. You never touch
those computers directly — you log into a small *login node*, describe the work you want
done, and a scheduler runs it on a *compute node* when resources free up. The golden rule:
**log in on the login node, but do the computing on compute nodes.**
:::

## The one-sentence mental model

MedicineBow is not "a really big computer." It is a few hundred ordinary Linux servers
("nodes") wired together, all mounting the same shared filesystems, all managed by a
program that decides whose job runs where and when. That program is the **scheduler**
(here, [Slurm](https://slurm.schedmd.com/)). Learning the cluster is mostly learning to
work *with* the scheduler instead of against it.

## Login nodes vs. compute nodes

There are two kinds of machines you'll deal with, and confusing them is the most common
beginner mistake.

**Login nodes** (`mblog1`, `mblog2`) are the front door. When you `ssh` in or open a
terminal in the web portal, you land here. Login nodes are *shared by everyone at once* —
dozens of people are on the same machine editing files, submitting jobs, and moving data.
They are for lightweight work: editing scripts, managing files, compiling small things,
submitting jobs, checking on jobs.

**Compute nodes** are where actual computation happens. You never SSH to them directly.
Instead you ask the scheduler for one (or many), and it gives you exclusive, accounted-for
access for a bounded amount of time. A compute node on MedicineBow is a serious machine —
the default `mb` nodes have **96 CPU cores and ~1 TB of RAM each**, and the GPU nodes carry
up to **8 NVIDIA H100s**. Your laptop has, what, 8 cores?

::: {.callout-important}
## The cardinal sin: computing on a login node
If you run a heavy job directly on `mblog1`/`mblog2` — a big simulation, a data-crunching
Python script, a multi-hour build — you slow the machine down for *everyone* trying to log
in and work. ARCC monitors this and will kill runaway login-node processes (and email you).

A useful rule of thumb: anything that takes more than a couple of minutes, or uses more
than a core or two, belongs in a Slurm job or an interactive session — never on the login
node. See @sec-why-scheduler.
:::

## Why share a machine at all?

Because the alternative is worse. If everyone had their own dedicated server, most servers
would sit idle most of the time while a few people occasionally needed far more than one
server could give. Pooling the hardware and scheduling access means:

- When you need 50 nodes for an ensemble, you can have them (briefly).
- When you need nothing, someone else uses the hardware you're not using.
- A fair-share accounting system stops any one person from hogging everything.

The cost of this deal is that you sometimes **wait in line**, and you have to **describe
your work up front** (how many cores, how much memory, how long). Most of this book is
about making those two things painless.

## What MedicineBow is, concretely

MedicineBow is a RHEL 9 Linux cluster. Its hardware is a mix of:

- **General CPU nodes** (the `mb` partition): 25 nodes, 96 cores and ~1 TB RAM each.
- **GPU nodes**: H100, L40S, A30, A6000, and R6000 flavors — for ML, PINNs, and anything
  CUDA.
- **Absorbed older clusters**: the retired *Teton*, *Beartooth*, and *WildIris* clusters
  now live on as large partitions inside MedicineBow. Teton alone is ~250 nodes.
- **Investor ("condo") nodes**: hardware bought by specific research groups, which the
  rest of us can borrow when it's idle — with the catch that the owner can reclaim it and
  bump your job (see @sec-preemption).

You don't need to memorize any of this yet. The partition chapter (@sec-partitions) lays
out exactly which hardware to ask for, and the queue-times chapter (@sec-queue-times) tells
you which choices leave you waiting versus running now.
